synopsis: Exhaustive field coverage of more than 7,000 testing strata is infeasible; a 1% miss-rate claim in each of 20 critical strata at 95% one-sided confidence requires about 6,000 zero-miss trials, making simulation or hardware-in-the-loop essential for volume, alongside a credibility argument [f132, f6654, f6925]. Simulation can establish logic, timing and braking-envelope correctness across large parameter sweeps, but behavioural, sensor and closed-loop simulation must not be treated as interchangeable, and semantic object injection assumes perception has succeeded [f909, f462, f5779]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, abstract closed-loop machine-and-site simulation is considered realistic by mid-2027; documented reductions in physical testing relied on years of prior investment or narrow operating envelopes, and no published manufacturer statement confirming shortened off-road validation time was found [f844, f1256, f257]. Credibility remains limited by poorly validated glare and reflective-clothing effects, missing evidence for mud or dirt on radar, and uncertainty about predicting combined environmental and machine effects; calibration in fog and rain chambers and field validation are recommended [f4406, f4678, f9343, f10574]. Vehicle-and-environment simulation does not represent operator adaptation and related behavioural changes, so human delay should be explored through uncertain parameters or distributions, while behaviour change requires months of field time [f8206, f3478, f11858]. ISO 18497-4:2024 explicitly includes simulation as a verification method for agricultural machinery, but simulator errors can mask defects when results become safety evidence; recommended safeguards include upgrade regression testing and, as a fallback, using simulation for screening while retaining physical verification for acceptance [f5275, f10543, f8897, f9697].

Both place approximately 6,000 zero-miss trials beyond practical physical testing.
